parts.title: Part II -- Short Answer (Reference to Context)
parts.instruction: Answer any 7 of the following 10 questions. Read the lines carefully and answer in one or two sentences each.

questions.verse: "She was like the winter landscape in the mountains, an expanse of pure white serenity breathing peace and contentment."

subs.q: (a) Name the figure of speech used in this line.
subs.a: The figure of speech is Simile -- the grandmother is compared to the winter landscape in the mountains using the word "like."

subs.q: (b) What qualities of the grandmother does this comparison highlight?
subs.a: The comparison highlights her purity, serenity, peace and contentment -- she radiated an overwhelming calmness, vast and unshakeable like a snow-covered mountain.

questions.verse: "The common link of friendship was snapped."

subs.q: (a) When exactly was this link snapped?
subs.a: The link was snapped when the author went to university and was given a room of his own -- he no longer shared time or space with his grandmother.

subs.q: (b) What does the word "snapped" suggest about the break in their relationship?
subs.a: "Snapped" suggests the break was sudden and complete -- not a slow fading but a sharp, clean cut, like a thread pulled too tight.

questions.verse: "Silently she kissed my forehead, and when I left I cherished the moist imprint as perhaps the last sign of physical contact between us."

subs.q: (a) Where was the author going and for how long?
subs.a: The author was going abroad for further studies and would be away for five years.

subs.q: (b) Why does the author use the word "perhaps" in this line?
subs.a: "Perhaps" shows the author's uncertainty -- he feared she might not be alive when he returned due to her old age, so the kiss might truly be their last physical contact.

questions.verse: "Her lips stopped moving and the rosary fell from her lifeless fingers."

subs.q: (a) What event does this line describe?
subs.a: This line describes the death of the grandmother -- the moment her lips stopped moving in prayer and the rosary fell from her hands, signalling that she was gone.

subs.q: (b) Why does the author choose this image rather than describing her death directly?
subs.a: The falling rosary is a powerful symbolic image -- it shows her death through the end of her prayer rather than through drama. The restraint makes the moment more moving and dignified.

questions.verse: "The sparrows took no notice of the bread."

subs.q: (a) Who threw the bread and why?
subs.a: The author's mother threw the bread, broken into little crumbs the way grandmother used to, feeling sorry for the thousands of sparrows that had gathered silently in the room.

subs.q: (b) What is the significance of the sparrows refusing to eat the bread?
subs.a: The sparrows' refusal shows they came not for food but for the grandmother herself -- it is their silent mourning, the most powerful tribute in the entire story.

questions.verse: "My grandmother and I were good friends. My parents left me with her when they went to live in the city and we were constantly together."

subs.q: (a) What does calling her a "good friend" rather than a grandmother suggest?
subs.a: It suggests their bond was one of genuine companionship -- mutual enjoyment of each other's company -- not just the formal love of grandparent and grandchild.

subs.q: (b) How did they spend their time together in the village?
subs.a: They shared every morning together -- she bathed him, fed him, walked with him to school, sat reading scriptures while he studied, and walked back feeding the village dogs.

questions.verse: "She did not pray. She collected the women of the neighbourhood, got an old drum and started to sing."

subs.q: (a) On what occasion did this happen?
subs.a: This happened on the evening of the author's return from five years abroad -- she was overjoyed at his homecoming.

subs.q: (b) Why is this moment significant in the story?
subs.a: It is the only time in the entire story that she skips her prayers -- showing her joy was so overwhelming that it overflowed even beyond her deepest daily devotion.

questions.verse: "She could never have been pretty; but she was always beautiful."

subs.q: (a) Explain the difference between being "pretty" and being "beautiful" as the author uses it here.
subs.a: "Pretty" refers to physical attractiveness -- symmetrical features and youthful looks. "Beautiful" refers to inner character -- her purity, devotion, selflessness and love made her profoundly beautiful despite her wrinkled appearance.

subs.q: (b) What does this line tell us about the author's view of beauty?
subs.a: The author believes true beauty is not physical but spiritual and moral -- it comes from within, from how a person lives and loves, not from how they look.

questions.verse: "She said her morning prayer in a monotonous sing-song while she bathed and dressed me, in the hope that I would listen and get to know it by heart."

subs.q: (a) Did the author learn the prayer? Why or why not?
subs.a: No -- he listened because he loved her voice, but never bothered to learn the prayer. He enjoyed the sound without engaging with the content.

subs.q: (b) What does this moment reveal about the grandmother's character?
subs.a: It reveals her deep desire to pass on her faith and values to her grandson -- she was always hopeful, always trying to share what mattered most to her, even without forcing it.

questions.verse: "When we carried my grandmother's corpse off, they flew away quietly. Next morning the sweeper swept the bread crumbs into the dustbin."

subs.a: "They" refers to the thousands of sparrows who had gathered silently all over the grandmother's room and verandah after her death.

subs.q: (b) What is the effect of the final sentence about the sweeper and the bread crumbs?
subs.a: It creates a mood of quiet finality -- the untouched bread crumbs swept away represent the end of her presence in the house, a small but deeply poignant image of how life moves on after loss.

parts.title: Part III -- Short Essay / Para Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 7 of the following 10 questions in two or three sentences each. (Approx. 30-40 words per answer)

questions.q: Describe the physical appearance of the author's grandmother as portrayed in the story.
questions.ans: The grandmother was short, fat and slightly bent with one hand resting on her waist to balance her stoop. Her face was a criss-cross of wrinkles and her silver locks were scattered untidily over her pale, puckered face. Her lips constantly moved in inaudible prayer and she always wore spotless white. Though she could never have been pretty, she was always beautiful -- like the winter landscape in the mountains, an expanse of pure white serenity.

questions.q: How did the grandmother spend her days after the author went to university?
questions.ans: After the author went to university and got a room of his own, the common link of their friendship was snapped. The grandmother accepted her seclusion with resignation and rarely left her spinning-wheel to talk to anyone. From sunrise to sunset she sat spinning and reciting prayers. Only in the afternoon did she relax for a while to feed the sparrows in the verandah -- that half-hour was the happiest time of her day.

questions.q: What was the morning routine shared between the author and his grandmother in the village?
questions.ans: Every morning the grandmother woke the author up and said her morning prayer in a monotonous sing-song while bathing and dressing him. She fetched his wooden slate -- already washed and plastered with yellow chalk -- tied the inkpot and red pen in a bundle, and gave him breakfast of thick stale chapatti with butter and sugar. Then they walked to school together, with the grandmother carrying stale chapattis for the village dogs.

questions.q: How is school education in the village different from that in the city in the story?
questions.ans: In the village, the school was attached to the temple and the priest taught both the alphabet and the morning prayer -- God and learning existed together. Grandmother could sit inside and read scriptures while the author studied. In the city, he took a motor bus to an English school where western science -- gravity, Archimedes' Principle, the earth being round -- was taught. There was no teaching about God or scriptures, which distressed the grandmother deeply.

questions.q: What happened when the author returned home after five years abroad?
questions.ans: When the author returned after five years, the grandmother met him at the station and did not look a day older. That evening, a change came over her -- she did not pray. She collected the neighbourhood women, got an old dilapidated drum, and sang songs of the home-coming of warriors for several hours. They had to persuade her to stop. That was the first and only time he had known her not to pray. The next morning she fell ill.

questions.q: The grandmother was strong-minded. Give two instances from the story to justify this.
questions.ans: First: when the author went abroad for five years, she was not sentimental -- she came to the station, kissed him silently, and let him go without showing any emotion, her lips moving only in prayer. Second: when she was dying, she refused to waste her remaining hours in conversation. She ignored all protests from the family and lay peacefully telling her beads until her last breath. In both cases she chose spirit over sentiment -- showing remarkable inner strength.

questions.q: How did the sparrows mourn the grandmother's death?
questions.ans: When the family came to carry the grandmother's body for cremation, thousands of sparrows sat scattered all over her verandah and room in complete silence -- no chirruping at all. When the mother broke bread into crumbs the way the grandmother used to and threw it to them, the sparrows took no notice of the bread. When her corpse was carried off, they flew away quietly. The next morning the sweeper swept the untouched bread crumbs into the dustbin.

questions.q: Why did the grandmother disapprove of the music lessons? What does this tell us about her character?
questions.ans: When the author announced that music lessons were being given at school, the grandmother said nothing -- but her silence meant disapproval. To her, music was associated with dancing girls and disreputable people and had no place in respectable school education. She rarely talked to him much after that. This reveals her deep rootedness in tradition and her high moral standards -- she valued education that formed the whole person, not just the intellect.

questions.q: "She could never have been pretty; but she was always beautiful." Explain this statement.
questions.ans: The author draws a clear distinction between being "pretty" -- which is about physical appearance -- and being "beautiful" -- which is about inner character. Physically, the grandmother was short, fat, bent, and criss-crossed with wrinkles; she had never been pretty. But her constant devotion, her spotless white clothes, her selfless love, and the serenity she radiated made her profoundly beautiful. True beauty, Singh argues, is not in one's features but in one's soul.

questions.q: What does the story tell us about the changing nature of human relationships in modern life?
questions.ans: The story shows how education, cities, and ambitions quietly distance people from those who love them most. The grandmother and author's bond was closest in the village -- shared routines, shared school walks, shared meals. Each step of modernisation -- the city school, university, foreign studies -- pulled them further apart. Yet she never complained, never blamed. The story argues that modernity creates distances that love alone cannot always bridge -- a quiet, honest portrait of how the world leaves some people behind.

parts.title: Part IV -- Long Essay Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 5 of the following 7 questions in about 100-150 words each.

questions.q: 1. Write an essay on the character of the grandmother as portrayed in "The Portrait of a Lady." Refer to all three phases of the story in your answer.
questions.ans:
Khushwant Singh's grandmother is one of the most beautifully drawn characters in Indian English literature -- a woman who embodies devotion, selflessness and quiet strength across all three phases of her life.

In the village, she is the author's constant companion -- waking him, feeding him, walking with him to school, sitting beside him in spirit even when in a different room. She carries chapattis for the village dogs without being asked. Every act is an act of love.

In the city, as modernity slowly erases her role, she accepts her seclusion without a single word of protest. She spins. She prays. She feeds the sparrows. Her world shrinks, but her spirit does not.

When the author returns from abroad, her joy overflows so completely that she abandons her prayers for one evening and sings. And when death comes, she faces it as she faced life -- quietly, spiritually, without fuss.

The falling rosary, the silent sparrows -- these final images tell us everything. She was not just a grandmother. She was, as Singh says, always beautiful. And the story is his act of gratitude.

questions.q: 2. "The sparrows were the most honest mourners at the grandmother's funeral." Do you agree? Discuss the significance of the sparrows in the story.
questions.ans:
The sparrows appear at two key moments in the story -- during the grandmother's living years and at the moment of her death -- and both times they tell us more about her worth than any human character does.

During her years of isolation in the city, the sparrows were her only real companions. Every afternoon she sat in the verandah breaking bread into little bits, and hundreds of birds gathered around her -- perching on her legs, her shoulders, even her head -- creating what Singh calls "a veritable bedlam of chirruping." That half-hour was the happiest of her day.

At her death, the sparrows return -- not in noise but in silence. Thousands sat scattered in her room and verandah, not chirruping. When the mother threw bread crumbs, they took no notice. They had not come for food. They came for her.

Yes -- the sparrows were the most honest mourners. They could not speak, but their silence said what human language could not. Their refusal to eat is the story's most powerful moment -- pure, instinctive, unconditional grief. Unlike humans, they had no social obligation to mourn. They mourned because they meant it.

questions.q: 3. The story explores the theme of tradition versus modernity. How does Khushwant Singh present this conflict through the lives of the grandmother and the grandson?
questions.ans:
From the very first phase of the story, Khushwant Singh places tradition and modernity in quiet conflict with each other -- never in open battle, but in a steady, painful divergence.

The grandmother belongs entirely to the old world. The village school attached to the temple, where the priest taught both the alphabet and morning prayer, was her natural home. She could walk alongside the author's education, sit reading scriptures beside his classroom, share every morning of his learning. God and knowledge were not separate for her.

The city shatters this. The author's English school teaches the law of gravity, Archimedes' Principle, and the roundness of the world -- things she neither understood nor believed in. There was no teaching about God. She was distressed. And when music was added -- associated in her mind with disreputable people -- her silence said everything.

The author does not blame modernity. He does not blame tradition. He simply shows how each step forward -- city, university, foreign study -- carries the grandson further from the world his grandmother inhabits. The distance is nobody's fault. It is simply what life does.

And she, rooted in her tradition, adjusts without anger. She simply shrinks her world -- from village dogs to city sparrows -- and prays.

questions.q: 4. Write a character sketch of Khushwant Singh based on what you learn about him as a writer and as a narrator in "The Portrait of a Lady."
questions.ans:
Khushwant Singh reveals himself in "The Portrait of a Lady" as a writer of remarkable honesty, restraint and warmth -- and as a narrator who is not afraid to admit his own inadequacies.

As a writer, he does not sentimentalise. He describes his grandmother's death in a single line -- "her lips stopped moving and the rosary fell from her lifeless fingers." He trusts the image. He does not explain the grief. He does not manufacture tears. This restraint is the mark of a genuinely gifted writer.

As a narrator, he is disarmingly honest. He tells us he listened to her prayers because he loved her voice -- but never bothered to learn them. He does not pretend to have been a devoted grandson. He drifted. He had a room of his own. He went abroad. He simply tells us what happened -- and lets the reader feel the weight of what was lost without being instructed to feel it.

His love for the grandmother is evident in every sentence -- not proclaimed loudly, but present in the careful attention he pays to every detail. The yellow chalk on the slate. The moist imprint of the kiss. The untouched bread crumbs. These details only survive in memory because someone paid close, loving attention.

questions.q: 5. "The grandmother never asked for anything in return for her love." Discuss this statement with examples from the story.
questions.ans:
The defining quality of the grandmother's love in "The Portrait of a Lady" is its utter absence of demand. At every stage of the story, she gives without condition, adjusts without complaint, and lets go without resistance.

In the village, she gives everything -- her mornings, her walks, her prayers, her chapattis. She asks only that the author listen to her prayers as she dresses him -- and when he never learns them, she says nothing. She does not withdraw her love.

In the city, when the common link is snapped and she is left alone from sunrise to sunset, she does not seek his company. She does not sulk. She accepts her seclusion with resignation. She finds the sparrows.

When he goes abroad for five years -- an age at which she might reasonably have begged him to stay -- she comes to the station, offers a silent kiss, and lets him go. She is not even sentimental.

And when she is dying, she refuses to waste her remaining time in conversation that would make others feel better. She chooses prayer over comfort -- her own spiritual integrity over social expectation.

This is the purest form of love -- one that asks nothing, adapts to everything, and leaves quietly. Singh honours it by telling us honestly that he did not fully understand it until she was gone.

questions.q: 6. How does Khushwant Singh use imagery and symbolism to convey the character of the grandmother? Refer to at least three specific examples from the story.
questions.ans:
Khushwant Singh is a master of the telling detail -- he builds his grandmother's character not through abstract description but through concrete, resonant images that accumulate into a complete portrait.

The most powerful is the simile: "She was like the winter landscape in the mountains, an expanse of pure white serenity breathing peace and contentment." This single image does more than a paragraph of adjectives. We see her vastness, her stillness, her purity, her permanence -- all in one breath.

The rosary is the story's central symbol. It appears in every phase -- always in her hand, always being counted, her connection to God made physical and constant. When it falls from her lifeless fingers at her death, it signals not just the end of her life but the end of that continuous prayer that defined her entire existence.

The sparrows are perhaps the most complex symbol. They represent her gentle companionship, her quiet joy, her uncomplaining acceptance of a diminished world. And their silence at her death -- their refusal to eat the bread -- is the story's most powerful symbolic act. They mourn in a way no human character does.

Taken together, these images create a woman who is not described but felt -- present on the page long after the story ends.

questions.q: 7. Write a paragraph on what "The Portrait of a Lady" teaches us about the importance of elders in our lives.
questions.ans:
"The Portrait of a Lady" is, at its heart, a story about what we lose when we stop paying attention to the people who love us most -- and what we gain, at least in memory, when we finally do.

The grandmother gave the author everything -- structure, warmth, routine, spiritual grounding, unconditional love. She woke him, fed him, walked with him, prepared his school materials, sat beside his learning, fed the village animals on his behalf. She was the backbone of his childhood, the constant thread running through every morning of his formative years.

And yet -- as life moved forward -- he drifted. The city school, the university, the foreign trip all pulled him away. Not out of cruelty, but out of living. And she, without a word of reproach, let him go.

What the story teaches us is not that modernity is wrong or that we must stay rooted. It teaches us to pay attention while we still can. To notice the moist kiss. To hear the rosary. To watch the sparrows while she feeds them. Because one morning, without warning, the rosary will fall and the sparrows will be silent.

Elders do not ask to be celebrated. They ask only to be seen. And this story is Khushwant Singh seeing his grandmother -- fully, honestly, gratefully -- on the page.

parts.title: Part II -- Short Answer / Reference to Context
parts.instruction: Answer any 7 of the following 10 questions. Read the passage carefully and answer in one or two sentences.

questions.verse: The policeman on the beat moved up the avenue impressively. The impressiveness was habitual and not for show, for spectators were few.

subs.a: The policeman is Patrolman Jimmy Wells.

subs.q: (b) What does this description reveal about him?
subs.a: It reveals that he is disciplined, alert, and sincere in his duty, not merely acting impressive for others.

questions.verse: "I'm just waiting for a friend. It's an appointment made twenty years ago."

subs.a: Bob says these words to the policeman.
The appointment is important because it brings the two old friends together and creates the central conflict between friendship and duty.

questions.verse: The light showed a pale, square-jawed face with keen eyes, and a little white scar near his right eyebrow.

subs.q: (a) What light is referred to here?
subs.a: It is the light from the match Bob strikes to light his cigar.
This moment is significant because Jimmy sees Bob's face clearly and recognizes him as the man wanted by Chicago police.

questions.verse: "He always was the truest, staunchest old chap in the world."

subs.a: Jimmy Wells is being praised.
The irony is that Jimmy truly is staunch, but his loyalty to duty makes him arrange Bob's arrest.

questions.verse: "I came a thousand miles to stand in this door tonight..."

subs.q: (a) Why has the speaker travelled so far?
subs.a: Bob has travelled to keep the old appointment with Jimmy.

subs.q: (b) What does it reveal about Bob?
subs.a: It shows Bob's emotional loyalty, but also his pride in dramatic gestures and his confidence that Jimmy will come.

questions.verse: There was now a fine, cold drizzle falling, and the wind had risen from its uncertain puffs into a steady blow.

subs.a: A lonely, suspenseful mood is created.

subs.q: (b) How does the weather support the story?
subs.a: The cold drizzle and wind make the meeting feel tense, uncertain, and suitable for a hidden arrest.

questions.verse: "Is that you, Bob?" he asked, doubtfully.

subs.a: The tall plainclothes policeman asks this question.
The word keeps suspense alive because the man is pretending to be Jimmy while confirming Bob's identity.

questions.verse: "Twenty years is a long time, but not long enough to change a man's nose from a Roman to a pug."

subs.a: Bob says this.
He realizes that the tall man walking with him is not Jimmy Wells.

questions.verse: "It sometimes changes a good man into a bad one."

subs.a: The plainclothes policeman says this line.
It means time may not change a nose, but it can change a person's character and moral path.

questions.verse: "Somehow I couldn't do it myself, so I went around and got a plainclothes man to do the job."

subs.a: Jimmy Wells wrote the note.

subs.q: (b) What does it reveal about Jimmy?
subs.a: It reveals that Jimmy is both emotionally loyal and professionally honest; he cannot free Bob, but cannot arrest him personally either.

parts.title: Part III -- Short Essay / Paragraph Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 7 of the following 10 questions in two or three sentences. (Approx. 30-40 words per answer)

questions.q: Describe the appearance of Bob.
questions.ans: Bob had a pale, square-jawed face with keen eyes and a little white scar near his right eyebrow. His diamond scarf pin and handsome watch showed wealth, pride, and love of display.

questions.q: What was the policeman's routine on the beat?
questions.ans: The policeman walked along the avenue, trying doors, twirling his club, and watching the street carefully. His actions showed that he was alert, responsible, and sincere in his duty.

questions.q: Compare Bob's view of the West and Jimmy's view of New York.
questions.ans: Bob believed the West sharpened a man and helped him make his fortune. Jimmy, however, loved New York and stayed there. Their choices show ambition on one side and rooted loyalty on the other.

questions.q: Explain Jimmy's strongest character trait with evidence.
questions.ans: Jimmy's strongest trait is duty-consciousness. Though Bob was his old friend, he did not let personal affection protect a wanted criminal. He arranged the arrest through a plainclothes policeman.

questions.q: Why is the drug store scene significant?
questions.ans: The drug store scene is significant because the electric lights reveal the tall man's face. Bob realizes he is not Jimmy, and the story moves from friendly reunion to arrest.

questions.q: How is loyalty shown in the story?
questions.ans: Loyalty is shown when both men keep the twenty-year appointment. However, Jimmy's loyalty is higher because he is loyal not only to friendship but also to law and duty.

questions.q: What happened when Bob lit his cigar?
questions.ans: When Bob lit his cigar, the match showed his face clearly. Jimmy recognized him as the man wanted in Chicago, and this small action silently changed the whole meeting.

questions.q: Explain the line "It sometimes changes a good man into a bad one."
questions.ans: The line means time may not change physical identity completely, but it can change moral character. Bob, once Jimmy's close friend, has become a criminal wanted by the police.

questions.q: What lesson does the story teach?
questions.ans: The story teaches that duty and honesty must stand above personal attachment. True friendship should not mean supporting wrongdoing, especially when society's safety is involved.

questions.q: How is the story relevant to modern life?
questions.ans: The story is relevant today because people still face conflicts between friendship and responsibility. It reminds us not to hide a friend's wrong actions, but to guide or stop them.

parts.title: Part IV -- Long Essay Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 5 of the following 7 questions. Each answer should be about 100-150 words.

questions.q: Compare and contrast Jimmy Wells and Bob.
questions.ans: Jimmy Wells and Bob were once close friends, raised in New York like brothers, but twenty years changes the direction of their lives. Bob goes West to make his fortune and becomes proud, showy, and finally criminal. His diamond pin, handsome watch, and boastful speech reveal success mixed with egotism. Jimmy stays in New York and becomes a policeman. He is loyal enough to keep the appointment exactly on time, but he is also dutiful enough to act when he recognizes Bob as the man wanted in Chicago. Bob values personal success; Jimmy values moral responsibility. Through them, O. Henry shows that friendship is meaningful, but character is proved by difficult choices.

questions.q: Duty is the central theme of the story. Explain.
questions.ans: Duty is the central theme of "After Twenty Years" because the climax depends on Jimmy Wells's moral choice. Jimmy and Bob had been close friends and had promised to meet after twenty years. Jimmy keeps the promise and arrives on time, which proves his loyalty. But when Bob lights his cigar, Jimmy recognizes him as the wanted criminal from Chicago. At that moment, he must choose between saving his friend and serving the law. He cannot arrest Bob personally because of old affection, so he brings a plainclothes man. This shows that real duty may be painful, but it must not be abandoned.

questions.q: Explain the significance of light in the story.
questions.ans: Light is an important symbol in "After Twenty Years." At first, the street is dark, rainy, and almost empty, which creates mystery. Bob waits in the doorway of a darkened hardware store, and his real identity is hidden. When he strikes a match to light his cigar, the small flame reveals his face to Jimmy. Later, the bright electric lights of the drug store reveal that the tall man is not Jimmy Wells. In both cases, light brings truth. O. Henry uses light to move the story from appearance to reality, from sentimental reunion to the shocking discovery of crime and duty.

questions.q: Compare Bob's past friendship with his present identity.
questions.ans: In the past, Bob was Jimmy Wells's closest friend. They were raised in New York like brothers, dined together at Big Joe Brady's, and made a sincere promise to meet after twenty years. That past shows warmth, trust, and youthful hope. In the present, Bob has become "Silky" Bob, a wanted man whom Chicago police are searching for. He is wealthy and confident, but his success is morally doubtful. This contrast between past affection and present crime gives the story its emotional force. O. Henry shows that memory may remain beautiful, even when a person has changed for the worse.

questions.q: Do you agree that Jimmy Wells is a true friend?
questions.ans: I agree that Jimmy Wells is a true friend, but he is not a blind friend. He keeps the twenty-year appointment and comes to meet Bob exactly as promised. This proves that he has not forgotten their bond. However, when he recognizes Bob as a wanted criminal, he does not misuse friendship to protect him. At the same time, he cannot arrest Bob with his own hands, which shows his emotional pain. A false friend might either betray the law or act cruelly. Jimmy does neither. He chooses duty, but his note reveals that he still remembers friendship.

questions.q: How does O. Henry create suspense and surprise?
questions.ans: O. Henry creates suspense through setting, dialogue, and hidden identity. The story begins on a cold, nearly empty avenue, where a policeman moves carefully along his beat. Bob's explanation of a twenty-year appointment sounds both touching and suspicious. Details such as the scar, diamond pin, and handsome watch make readers wonder about his past. The tall man who arrives keeps his collar turned up, so his identity remains hidden. The drug store lights suddenly reveal that he is not Jimmy. Finally, Jimmy's note explains the truth. This twist makes readers reinterpret the whole story, which is O. Henry's special craft.

questions.q: How is the story relevant to modern life?
questions.ans: "After Twenty Years" is relevant to modern life because people still face conflicts between personal relationships and public responsibility. A person may discover that a close friend is doing something wrong, dishonest, or harmful. At such a moment, loyalty should not mean silence. Jimmy Wells teaches us that friendship must not be used to protect crime. He keeps his promise as a friend, but he also respects his duty as a policeman. The story reminds students that character is tested not when choices are easy, but when doing the right thing hurts.

parts.title: Part IV -- Long Essay Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 5 of the following 7 questions. Each answer should be about 100-150 words.

questions.q: Write a character essay on Mary Kom as seen in this lesson.
questions.ans: Mary Kom appears in this lesson as a determined, honest, and courageous sportsperson. She is selected for the World Women's Boxing Championships in Pennsylvania, but her journey begins with financial difficulty. Her father can collect only Rs. 2,000, and she travels only after others help her. In America, she faces jet lag, unfamiliar food, and strong opponents. Yet her fear quickly vanishes, and she tells herself that she can face anyone in the ring. Though she loses the final and wins silver, she gains confidence. Later, she continues winning titles and becomes "Queen of Boxing." Her life teaches perseverance, humility, and self-belief.

questions.q: Explain the theme of perseverance in "The Queen of Boxing."
questions.ans: Perseverance is the central theme of "The Queen of Boxing." Mary Kom's journey is filled with challenges, but she refuses to give up. Financial difficulty almost stops her USA trip, yet she accepts help and travels. Jet lag, unfamiliar surroundings, and loss of appetite trouble her, but she continues fighting. Even after losing the final to Hula Sahin, she does not allow disappointment to end her dream. Instead, she vows to bring back gold next time. Her later victories, including the world title retained in 2006, prove that perseverance turns defeat into preparation for success.

questions.q: Explain the significance of the boxing ring in the lesson.
questions.ans: The boxing ring is more than a sports space in this lesson; it is the place where Mary Kom discovers her own strength. Before facing new opponents, she has fear. Once she enters the ring and wins, that fear vanishes. The ring tests not only her physical ability but also her confidence, discipline, and courage. Her statement, "I can face anyone in the ring," shows that the ring becomes a symbol of self-belief. Even when she loses the final, the experience gives her conviction. Thus, the boxing ring represents struggle, learning, and transformation.

questions.q: Compare Mary Kom's struggle in Pennsylvania with her later success.
questions.ans: In Pennsylvania, Mary Kom is still at the beginning of her international journey. She faces financial difficulty, jet lag, unfamiliar food, weight loss, and the disappointment of losing gold. Yet she wins silver and gains the belief that she can take on any boxer. Her later success shows how important that first experience was. She wins several golds, retains world titles, receives a government job, and becomes known as "Queen of Boxing" and "Magnificent Mary." The contrast shows that early struggle can become the foundation for greatness when a person learns from it.

questions.q: Do you agree that lack of sponsorship affects sportspersons? Explain with reference to Mary Kom.
questions.ans: Yes, lack of sponsorship seriously affects sportspersons. Mary Kom's selection for the USA championship should have been a moment of joy, but it immediately became a financial worry. Her father could collect only Rs. 2,000, and she was anxious because America was expensive. Only after Onler, students, elders, and two MPs helped her could she travel. Later, even after winning silver, she wanted a job for long-term security. This proves that sportspersons need financial support, equipment, travel expenses, food, training, and stable income. Talent must be protected by proper sponsorship.

questions.q: How does Mary Kom's autobiographical style make the lesson powerful?
questions.ans: Mary Kom's autobiographical style makes the lesson powerful because she speaks directly from experience. She does not only list victories; she tells us about fear, worry, hunger, crying, gratitude, and determination. Her sentences such as "I can face anyone in the ring" and "I vowed that the next time I would bring back a gold" reveal her inner voice. The reader sees the person behind the medals. This honest style makes the lesson inspirational, because students understand that champions also face doubt and disappointment, but they continue with courage.

questions.q: How is "The Queen of Boxing" relevant to modern students?
questions.ans: "The Queen of Boxing" is relevant to modern students because it teaches how to face pressure, failure, and limited resources. Many students dream big but feel discouraged by money, competition, or fear of failure. Mary Kom's life shows that these problems are real, but they are not final. She accepts help, works hard, adapts to new situations, learns from defeat, and returns stronger. Her first silver medal becomes the starting point for later golds. The lesson encourages students to build confidence through effort and to remember that determination can change the direction of life.

questions.q: Describe the speaker's physical and emotional self-image.
questions.ans: The speaker describes his spirit as "limp and bashful" and his body as modest. He sees himself as unsuited for rough athletic competition, but he is honest and cheerful about it.

questions.q: What kind of life does the speaker prefer?
questions.ans: The speaker prefers the life of a spectator. He enjoys watching heroic deeds, buying tickets, and celebrating athletes, but he does not want to compete or suffer injuries.

questions.q: Compare athletes and the speaker.
questions.ans: Athletes are active, zealous, rough, and heroic. The speaker is cautious, shy, and humorous. He admires athletes deeply, but his common sense keeps him safely in the audience.

questions.q: What character trait does "prudence wins" reveal?
questions.ans: The phrase reveals the speaker's wisdom and self-control. He may feel tempted by athletic glory, but he lets caution and common sense decide his actions.

questions.q: What is the significance of calling for a doctor?

questions.q: How is the theme of admiration shown?

questions.q: What happens when ego struggles with prudence?
questions.ans: When ego struggles with prudence, prudence wins. The speaker chooses wisdom over the desire to exchange places with athletes and gain heroic glory.

questions.q: Explain "My limp and bashful spirit feeds / On other people's heroic deeds."
questions.ans: The speaker means that his weak and shy nature gains satisfaction by watching brave actions performed by others. He enjoys heroism safely as a spectator.

questions.q: What is the moral of the poem?
questions.ans: The poem teaches that one should understand oneself. We may admire others, but we need not imitate them if their path does not suit our nature.

questions.q: How is this poem relevant to students?
questions.ans: Students often compare themselves with others. This poem teaches them to appreciate others' talents without jealousy and to choose activities that match their strengths and comfort.

parts.title: Part IV -- Long Essay Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 5 of the following 7 questions. Each answer should be about 100-150 words.

questions.q: Write a character essay on the speaker of the poem.
questions.ans: The speaker of "Confessions of a Born Spectator" is humorous, honest, cautious, and self-aware. He admires athletes "with all my heart" and enjoys watching their heroic deeds. However, he knows that he is not suited for rough competition. He calls his spirit "limp and bashful" and gives thanks for his modest physique. His ego may be pleased by the thought of exchanging places with athletes, but prudence wins. He is willing to drink with athletes, eat with them, and buy expensive tickets to watch them, but he refuses to compete. His character teaches that self-knowledge is better than false heroism.

questions.q: Explain the theme of common sense versus ego.
questions.ans: The central theme of the poem is the victory of common sense over ego. The speaker sees athletes scoring, boxing, riding, and performing heroic deeds. Naturally, his ego might enjoy the thought of becoming one of them. Yet he also sees the other side of sports: swollen eyes, gnarled fists, snapped knees, cracked wrists, and doctors being called from the stands. He understands that glory often brings pain. Therefore, when a struggle begins between prudence and ego, prudence wins. Ogden Nash humorously shows that wisdom lies in knowing one's own limits.

questions.q: Explain the significance of sports injuries in the poem.
questions.ans: Sports injuries are an important image in the poem because they help the speaker justify his choice to remain a spectator. Nash mentions rough athletes who do not consider one another's feelings. He then gives vivid images such as swollen eyes, gnarled fists, snapped knees, and cracked wrists. These images are comic, but they are also meaningful. They remind us that games may look glorious from the outside, but players often face real pain. The injuries become a symbol of the physical cost of athletic fame. They make the speaker's cautious choice appear sensible, not cowardly.

questions.q: Compare the athlete and the spectator in the poem.
questions.ans: In the poem, athletes and the spectator are sharply contrasted. Athletes are energetic, zealous, brave, and physically active. They sweat for fun or hire, take the field in gaudy pomp, and perform heroic deeds. However, they also play roughly and suffer injuries. The spectator, on the other hand, is limp, bashful, cautious, and humorous. He admires athletes but does not want to become one of them. He enjoys their heroism from the safety of the stands. While athletes represent action and risk, the spectator represents observation and prudence. Nash makes both sides memorable through humour.

questions.q: Do you agree that the speaker is not a coward but a sensible person?
questions.ans: Yes, the speaker is not a coward but a sensible person. He never says that athletes are foolish or unworthy. In fact, he says, "With all my heart I do admire" them. This proves that he respects courage. However, he also understands that sports involve rough play and injuries. He does not pretend to be what he is not. His ego may want glory, but prudence wins. A coward hides fear; the speaker openly admits his preference with humour. His honesty and self-knowledge make him sensible. The poem encourages readers to respect their own nature.

questions.q: How does Ogden Nash use humour and sound in the poem?
questions.ans: Ogden Nash uses humour through exaggeration, playful rhyme, and comic contrast. The speaker admires athletes but describes their world through images of maiming, cracking vertebrae, snapped knees, and doctors in the stands. These details are serious in meaning but funny in presentation. Nash's rhymes such as jockey/hockey, enter/center, radium/stadium create a light musical effect. He also uses sound words like "snaps" and "cracks" to make injuries vivid. The speaker's offer to drink or eat with athletes, but never compete, creates a witty ending. Humour helps Nash teach wisdom without sounding serious or moralising.

questions.q: How is the poem relevant to modern life?
questions.ans: The poem is relevant to modern life because people often compare themselves with others and feel pressured to imitate them. Students may admire toppers, athletes, artists, or public speakers and feel that they must become the same. Ogden Nash reminds us that admiration does not require imitation. The speaker respects athletes but knows that he is happier as a spectator. This message is healthy and practical. Everyone has different strengths, interests, and limits. The poem teaches us to celebrate others without jealousy and to choose our own path with honesty, humour, and common sense.

questions.q: Describe Bertie's appearance and behaviour in the train.
questions.ans: Bertie was a young man of about twenty-two, with dark hair and fresh complexion. He looked smart but untidy, searched frantically, muttered, cursed, and seemed worried about his missing purse.

questions.q: What was Sletherby's purpose in visiting Brill Manor?
questions.ans: Sletherby visited Brill Manor to gain Mrs. Saltpen-Jago's goodwill. Her influence in Chalkshire could help him secure political nomination and advance his ambition to become a politician.

questions.q: Compare the Jago and Saltpen crests.
questions.ans: The Jago crest was a greyhound courant, while the Saltpen crest was a demi-lion holding a cross-crosslet. Bertie said the family had the right to use both crests.

questions.q: What character trait of Sletherby is revealed by his "trap"?
questions.ans: Sletherby's trap reveals his caution, suspicion, and pride. He does not want to be cheated, but he also enjoys the thought of proving himself clever and resourceful.

questions.q: Why is the car-door scene significant?
questions.ans: The car-door scene is significant because Sletherby sees both crests there. This proves that Bertie's explanation was true and begins the collapse of Sletherby's proud judgement.

questions.q: How is the theme of misjudgement shown?
questions.ans: Sletherby judges Bertie as a fraud using incomplete evidence. The crests and hair colour seem suspicious, but later both are explained. His confident judgement becomes completely wrong.

questions.q: What did Bertie do after Sletherby refused money?
questions.ans: Bertie opened the carriage door, pitched his suitcase on to the platform, and angrily reminded Sletherby about the three quid. When refused, he cursed furiously.

questions.q: Explain the title "A Shot in the Dark."
questions.ans: The title means a guess made without full knowledge. Sletherby's judgement of Bertie is exactly such a guess: clever-looking, but finally wrong and embarrassing.

questions.q: What is the lesson of the story?
questions.ans: The story teaches that one should not judge others too quickly. Observation is useful, but without full context, even clever people can misunderstand truth and act unfairly.

questions.q: How is the story relevant to modern life?
questions.ans: In modern life, people often judge others from small details, messages, or appearances. This story reminds us to verify facts before accusing someone or refusing genuine help.

parts.title: Part IV -- Long Essay Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 5 of the following 7 questions. Each answer should be about 100-150 words.

questions.q: Write a character essay on Philip Sletherby.
questions.ans: Philip Sletherby is an ambitious, cautious, and self-confident man. He travels to Brill Manor hoping to gain Mrs. Saltpen-Jago's goodwill for his political career. When Bertie asks for money, Sletherby does not immediately trust him. He tests Bertie by asking about the family crest and Mrs. Saltpen-Jago's appearance. This shows caution, but it also reveals pride. He refuses to lend money and imagines himself telling the story at dinner as proof of his astuteness. However, the two crests on the car and Claude People's words prove that Bertie was genuine. Sletherby's character teaches that cleverness without humility can become foolishness.

questions.q: Explain the theme of misjudgement in "A Shot in the Dark."
questions.ans: Misjudgement is the central theme of "A Shot in the Dark." Sletherby believes he is careful and observant, but he reaches a wrong conclusion from incomplete evidence. Bertie's claim about the demi-lion crest seems suspicious because Sletherby has seen a greyhound crest on Mrs. Saltpen-Jago's letter. Bertie's statement that his mother has dark brown hair also seems false because Sletherby has seen her as a blonde. Later, both details are explained: the family uses both crests, and Mrs. Saltpen-Jago had changed her hair colour only five weeks earlier. Saki humorously shows that partial truth can lead to complete error.

questions.q: Explain the significance of the two crests in the story.
questions.ans: The two crests are the most important symbols in the story. Sletherby has seen a greyhound courant on Mrs. Saltpen-Jago's notepaper. Bertie says his own crest is a demi-lion holding a cross-crosslet. This difference makes Sletherby suspicious. Bertie explains that the greyhound is the Jago crest and the demi-lion is the Saltpen crest, but Sletherby does not fully believe him. Later, on the car door, Sletherby sees both crests displayed together. This proves Bertie's explanation true and exposes Sletherby's mistake. The crests show how evidence can mislead when a person knows only part of the truth.

questions.q: Compare Bertie and Sletherby.
questions.ans: Bertie and Sletherby are very different in position and behaviour. Bertie is young, stranded, anxious, and untidy because he has left behind his purse. He speaks quickly and asks for money in desperation. Sletherby is older, ambitious, politically minded, and careful about social advantage. Bertie appears suspicious, but he is actually truthful. Sletherby appears clever and cautious, but his judgement is wrong. Bertie needs practical help; Sletherby wants to protect himself from being cheated. Through this contrast, Saki shows that appearances can deceive and that social confidence does not always mean wisdom.

questions.q: Do you agree that Sletherby was right to be cautious?
questions.ans: Sletherby was right to be cautious, but wrong to be proud and final in his judgement. Bertie was a stranger in a railway carriage asking for three pounds. Any sensible person would think carefully before lending money. Sletherby's questions about the crest and Mrs. Saltpen-Jago's appearance were reasonable. However, he treated partial evidence as complete proof. He refused Bertie harshly and imagined receiving applause for his clever trap. Later he learnt that Bertie had told the truth. Therefore, caution was justified, but his overconfidence and lack of compassion made him unfair.

questions.q: How does Saki use irony and humour in the story?
questions.ans: Saki uses irony and humour by making Sletherby's cleverness turn against him. At first, the reader is encouraged to suspect Bertie. His frantic searching, request for money, and convenient story all seem doubtful. Sletherby's investigation appears intelligent when he notices the crest and hair-colour differences. The humour deepens when Sletherby proudly imagines telling the story at dinner. Then the twist arrives: both crests appear on the car door, and Mrs. Saltpen-Jago had only recently become blonde. The man who thought he had exposed a fraud has actually rejected a genuine plea. This reversal is classic Saki irony.

questions.q: How is the story relevant to modern life?
questions.ans: "A Shot in the Dark" is relevant to modern life because people still judge others from incomplete evidence. Today, a message, photograph, accent, clothing style, or small inconsistency can make us suspect someone. Like Sletherby, we may feel clever when we think we have discovered the truth. But the story reminds us that facts need context. Bertie's details sounded false only because Sletherby did not know the whole background. The lesson is practical: be cautious, but also be humble. Before accusing someone or refusing help, we should verify carefully and remember that appearances can mislead.

parts.title: Part II -- Reference to Context
parts.instruction: Answer any 7 of the following 10 questions. Read the extract carefully and answer in one or two sentences.

questions.verse:
Once upon a time, son
They used to laugh with their hearts
And laugh with their eyes:
But now they only laugh with their teeth
While their ice-block-cold eyes
Search behind my shadow.

subs.q: (a) Who is the narrator speaking to, and what does "laugh with their hearts" mean?
subs.a: The narrator is speaking to his young son. "Laugh with their hearts" means to laugh genuinely, with true joy and sincere emotion, as opposed to merely performing a smile for social appearance.

subs.q: (b) What does the image "ice-block-cold eyes" reveal about the people described?
subs.a: "Ice-block-cold eyes" reveals that the people's emotions are frozen and absent -- their eyes betray no warmth or genuine feeling. While their faces perform friendliness, their eyes expose cold calculation and self-interest.

questions.verse:
There was a time indeed
They used to shake hands with their hearts
But that's gone, son
Now they shake hands without hearts
While their left hands search
My empty pockets.

subs.q: (a) Identify the contrast the narrator draws between past and present handshakes.
subs.a: In the past, handshakes were warm and sincere -- "with their hearts." In the present, the right hand goes through the motion of greeting while the left hand secretly reaches into pockets, assessing the narrator's wealth.

subs.q: (b) What is the significance of "my empty pockets"?
subs.a: "My empty pockets" shows that the narrator has nothing material to offer. The people who search his pockets find nothing, yet they still perform friendship -- suggesting hypocrisy has become so habitual it continues even when there is nothing to be gained.

questions.verse:
"Feel at home!", "Come again":
They say, and when I come
Again and feel
At home, once, twice
There will be no thrice --
For then I find doors shut on me.

subs.q: (a) What happens when the narrator visits someone for the third time?
subs.a: When the narrator visits for the third time, he finds the door shut on him. Despite warm invitations -- "Feel at home!" and "Come again!" -- the welcome was never genuine; the words were empty social formulas.

subs.q: (b) Explain the irony in the expressions "Feel at home!" and "doors shut on me."
subs.a: The irony is devastating: the words that promise belonging ("Feel at home!") are followed by the action of exclusion ("doors shut on me"). The exclamatory warmth of the invitation is directly contradicted by the reality of the shut door.

questions.verse:
And I have learned too
To laugh with only my teeth
And shake hands without my heart
I have also learned to say "Goodbye"
When I mean "Good-riddance":
To say "Glad to meet you"
Without being glad; and to say "It's been
Nice talking to you", after being bored.

subs.q: (a) What does the narrator confess in these lines?
subs.a: The narrator confesses that he himself has adopted the very hypocrisy he had been criticising. He too laughs without feeling, shakes hands without warmth, and uses social pleasantries that are the opposite of his private feelings.

subs.q: (b) What is the effect of listing "Goodbye / Good-riddance," "Glad to meet you / without being glad"?
subs.a: The paired contrasts create a powerful accumulating effect. Each pair exposes one more layer of the narrator's own hypocrisy, building into an overwhelming catalogue of dishonesty that makes his self-indictment the emotional centrepiece of the poem.

questions.verse:
So I have learnt many things, son
I have learned to wear many faces
Like dresses - home face,
Office face, street face, host face,
Cocktail face, with all their conforming smiles
Like a fixed portrait smile.

subs.q: (a) What does the simile "wear many faces like dresses" mean?
subs.a: The simile compares the narrator's social personas to clothing. Just as one changes clothes for different occasions, the narrator changes his expression to suit different social contexts, implying that identity has become as changeable and superficial as what one wears.

subs.q: (b) Explain "conforming smiles like a fixed portrait smile."
subs.a: A portrait smile is frozen and painted -- it never changes or responds to anything real. "Conforming smiles" conform to social expectations rather than genuine feeling. Comparing them to a portrait smile means these expressions are lifeless performances, as fixed and artificial as paint on a canvas.

questions.verse:
But believe me, son
I want to be what I used to be
When I was like you. I want
To unlearn all these muting things.

subs.q: (a) What does the narrator mean by "I want to be what I used to be / When I was like you"?
subs.a: The narrator wants to return to the state of innocent authenticity he had when he was a child like his son -- before society taught him to perform and pretend. He sees his child as a mirror of his former self.

subs.q: (b) What are "these muting things" and why does the narrator want to unlearn them?
subs.a: "Muting things" are the social performances -- fake smiles, insincere handshakes, hollow pleasantries -- that the narrator has learned as an adult. They "mute" him by silencing his genuine emotions; he wants to unlearn them because they have replaced feeling with social calculation.

questions.verse:
Most of all, I want to relearn
How to laugh, for my laugh in the mirror
Shows only my teeth like a snake's bare fangs!

subs.q: (a) Why does the narrator want to "relearn" how to laugh?
subs.a: The narrator wants to relearn genuine laughter because when he laughs before the mirror, he sees only bared teeth like a snake's fangs -- with no warmth or joy behind them. His laughter has become the same hollow performance he once criticised in others.

subs.q: (b) Name and explain the figure of speech in "like a snake's bare fangs."
subs.a: The figure of speech is a simile -- the narrator's hollow smile is compared to a snake's bare fangs using "like." Snake fangs have the shape of teeth but are weapons, not expressions of warmth, just as the narrator's smile looks like a smile but carries none of its genuine human feeling.

questions.verse:
So show me, son,
How to laugh; show me how
I used to laugh and smile
Once upon a time when I was like you.

subs.q: (a) What is unusual about the narrator asking his son for guidance?
subs.a: It is unusual because adults are expected to teach children, not the other way round. The father reverses traditional roles by asking his young son to show him how to laugh, suggesting that the child possesses a wisdom of innocence that the adult has lost.

subs.q: (b) How does the phrase "once upon a time" at the end echo the opening of the poem?
subs.a: "Once upon a time" appears in the title, first line, and final stanza, creating a circular structure. The fairy-tale phrase signals that the innocence the narrator seeks belongs to a lost world now accessible only through his child, reinforcing the theme of irreversible loss.

questions.verse:
I have also learned to say "Goodbye"
When I mean "Good-riddance":
To say "Glad to meet you"
Without being glad.

subs.q: (a) Name the figure of speech used when "Goodbye" is contrasted with "Good-riddance."
subs.a: The figure of speech is antithesis -- two opposing ideas ("Goodbye," a polite farewell, versus "Good-riddance," relief at being rid of someone) are placed in direct contrast to expose the gap between social performance and private truth.

subs.q: (b) What does this passage reveal about the nature of social language?
subs.a: This passage reveals that social language has been severed from genuine meaning. Words like "Goodbye" and "Glad to meet you" are spoken as automatic formulas regardless of what the speaker feels -- language has become a tool of concealment rather than expression.

questions.verse:
They used to shake hands with their hearts
But that's gone, son
Now they shake hands without hearts
While their left hands search
My empty pockets.

subs.q: (a) To whom is the narrator speaking, and what is the tone of these lines?
subs.a: The narrator is speaking to his young son. The tone is mournful and disillusioned -- he laments that the genuine warmth of greeting ("shake hands with their hearts") is "gone," replaced by calculating performance that conceals self-interest.

subs.q: (b) What does "left hands search my empty pockets" suggest about modern relationships?
subs.a: The image suggests that modern relationships are fundamentally transactional. While the right hand performs friendship, the left simultaneously probes for material benefit. The "empty pockets" add pathos -- the narrator has nothing to offer, yet the performance continues, showing hypocrisy has become purely habitual.

parts.title: Part III -- Short Essay / Paragraph Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 7 of the following 10 questions in two or three sentences. (Approx. 30-40 words per answer)

questions.q: Describe what the narrator means when he says people used to "laugh with their hearts" and "laugh with their eyes."
questions.ans: The narrator means that in the past, laughter was completely genuine -- it arose from real joy felt in the heart and was visible even in the eyes, which would light up with authentic warmth. Both inner feeling and outward expression were fully sincere, with nothing hidden or performed.

questions.q: What daily social rituals does the narrator accuse people of performing insincerely?
questions.ans: The narrator accuses people of performing laughter, handshakes, and hospitality insincerely. They smile without feeling, shake hands while mentally assessing what they can gain, and invite guests warmly only to shut the door on them by the third visit.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's description of genuine laughter in the past with his hollow laughter in the present.
questions.ans: In the past, people laughed with their hearts and eyes -- the whole being participated in real joy. In the present, the narrator himself laughs with only his teeth, baring them like a snake's fangs before a mirror that reflects no warmth -- a performance that mimics laughter without any of its life.

questions.q: What specific character trait does the narrator reveal about himself in stanza 4?
questions.ans: In stanza 4, the narrator reveals that he has become a hypocrite -- the very thing he was criticising. He confesses with painful honesty that he says "Goodbye" when he means "Good-riddance" and performs pleasantries he does not mean, exposing his own moral corruption.

questions.q: Explain the significance of the narrator visiting someone "once, twice" and then finding "doors shut" on the third visit.
questions.ans: The significance is that the warm invitations -- "Feel at home!" and "Come again!" -- were never genuine; they had an invisible expiry date. The shut door on the third visit exposes the hollowness of modern hospitality, where words of welcome are automatic formulas with no real intention behind them.

questions.q: How does the theme of hypocrisy run through the entire poem?
questions.ans: Hypocrisy runs through every stanza as the poem moves systematically through social rituals -- laughter, handshakes, hospitality, farewells -- showing each one hollowed out by pretence. The theme climaxes when the narrator admits he has himself become hypocritical, and ends with his desperate plea to recover genuine feeling.

questions.q: What does the narrator mean by learning to wear "many faces like dresses"?
questions.ans: The narrator means that he has learned to change his personality to suit different social settings -- a home face, office face, street face -- just as one changes outfits for different occasions. This comparison implies that identity has become a costume adjusted for social convenience, not a truth.

questions.q: Explain the line: "I want to unlearn all these muting things."
questions.ans: "Muting things" are the social performances that silence genuine emotion -- fake smiles, hollow handshakes, insincere words. The narrator wants to shed them because they have suppressed his authentic voice. "Unlearn" is significant: these are not natural qualities but things he was taught by the world around him.

questions.q: What moral or message does the poem convey to the reader?
questions.ans: The poem's central message is that modern society corrupts even good people into social performers who have lost touch with genuine feeling. The narrator's plea to his son -- 'show me how to laugh' -- suggests that innocence and authenticity are more valuable than all the social sophistication the adult world demands.

questions.q: How is the child in the poem relevant to a modern student's own life?
questions.ans: The child represents what every student still holds within -- the ability to laugh genuinely and mean what they say. As students navigate social pressures and social media performance, Okara's warning resonates: the world will teach you to wear many faces. The poem asks: which face is really yours?

parts.title: Part IV -- Long Essay Questions
parts.instruction: Answer any 5 of the following 7 questions. Each answer should be about 100-150 words.

questions.q: Write a character essay on the narrator of "Once Upon a Time." Cover all aspects of his character across the full poem.
questions.ans: The narrator of "Once Upon a Time" is a deeply self-aware father figure who serves as both observer and confessor. He begins the poem as a critic of modern society, cataloguing with precision the ways people have abandoned genuine warmth -- their laughter hollow, their handshakes calculating, their welcomes false. What makes him a remarkable literary character, however, is that he does not remain safely outside this critique. By stanza four, he confesses that he too has learned to laugh with only his teeth, to say "Goodbye" when he means "Good-riddance," and to wear multiple social faces like changing costumes. He does not excuse himself or blame circumstance; he simply admits the truth. This honesty is his defining quality. Underneath the social performance, he retains genuine self-awareness and a powerful longing for the authentic self he once was. His turning to his son at the end -- asking the child to teach him how to laugh -- reveals both humility and hope.

questions.q: "Once Upon a Time" is a poem about the loss of authentic human connection in modern society. Discuss with reference to specific images and events in the poem.
questions.ans: Gabriel Okara's "Once Upon a Time" traces the death of authentic human connection through three key social rituals: laughter, the handshake, and hospitality. Laughter -- once a full-bodied expression of joy, engaging heart and eyes alike -- has been reduced to the baring of teeth while ice-block-cold eyes calculate what can be gained. The handshake -- once a gesture of genuine warmth -- has become a probe: the right hand extends in greeting while the left secretly searches empty pockets for signs of wealth. Hospitality -- once real and lasting -- has an invisible expiry: 'Come again!' is said with no intention of meaning it beyond a second visit, and the door is shut on the third. The poem's most devastating point is that even the narrator has been transformed. He too wears many faces like dresses -- a home face, an office face, a cocktail face -- each with its conforming smile.

questions.q: Analyse the significance of the image of the snake's fangs in "Once Upon a Time" and what it reveals about the narrator's condition.
questions.ans: The image of the snake's bare fangs appears at the climax of the poem, when the narrator looks at his own laugh in the mirror and sees nothing but bared teeth -- 'like a snake's bare fangs.' This simile is among the most carefully chosen in the poem, and its significance operates on several levels. First, it is physically precise: snake fangs, though shaped like teeth, are weapons -- hollow tubes through which venom is injected. They resemble a smile but carry destruction. The narrator's social smile similarly has the shape of warmth but none of its content. Second, the mirror is the one audience before which no performance is possible. What he sees is not joy but threat -- something predatory and cold where genuine happiness should be. Third, the image marks the emotional lowest point of the poem -- the moment the narrator fully recognises his own transformation, driving his desperate plea to his son in the final stanza.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the world "once upon a time" with the world the narrator inhabits now. What has been lost and what remains?
questions.ans: The world "once upon a time" was a world of wholeness: people laughed with their hearts and their eyes together, shook hands with genuine warmth, welcomed guests with real intention. It was a world where language matched feeling -- where "Goodbye" meant farewell and "Come again" meant a real invitation. The world the narrator inhabits now is a world of fragments and performances. The face has been disconnected from the feeling. The word has been disconnected from the meaning. Social rituals continue -- handshakes, welcomes, farewells -- but emptied of their content, repurposed as tools of social climbing and self-interest. Yet something remains: the child. The son is still in the world Okara mourns -- still laughing with his whole face, still meaning what he says. He represents the proof that authenticity has not been destroyed, only lost. In that fact lies the poem's quiet hope.

questions.q: "Face is the index of the mind." Does this adage concur with the views of the poet in "Once Upon a Time"? Discuss.
questions.ans: The adage "face is the index of the mind" suggests that what shows on the face accurately reflects what is happening in the mind. Okara's poem argues precisely the opposite, and does so systematically. His characters wear faces completely disconnected from their minds. The smiling face conceals cold calculation in the eyes. The extended hand of greeting hides the other hand reaching for the pocket. The effusive welcome conceals an intention to shut the door by the third visit. The narrator himself says "It's been nice talking to you" while inwardly relieved to escape a boring conversation. In Okara's world, the face has become the mask over the mind rather than its reflection. The only exception is the child -- whose face still matches his feeling. The adage applies to the child. In the adult world Okara portrays, the adage has been systematically and deliberately overturned.

questions.q: Examine how Gabriel Okara uses language and literary devices to convey the theme of hypocrisy in "Once Upon a Time."
questions.ans: Okara builds his indictment of hypocrisy through three principal literary strategies. First, he uses concrete physical imagery -- ice-block-cold eyes, empty pockets, shut doors, snake fangs -- to make abstract social dishonesty tangible and visceral. Each image gives hypocrisy a body; the reader cannot dismiss it as a vague concept. Second, he employs antithesis systematically: "laugh with their hearts" versus "laugh with their teeth"; "shake hands with their hearts" versus "shake hands without hearts"; "Goodbye" versus "Good-riddance." These paired contrasts expose the gap between social performance and private truth. Third, and most powerfully, he uses confession. By making the narrator both the critic and the guilty party, Okara refuses to let the poem settle into comfortable moralising. The narrator sees the problem and is part of it -- which makes the critique universal rather than judgmental.

questions.q: How relevant is "Once Upon a Time" to modern life and to the experiences of young people today?
questions.ans: "Once Upon a Time" speaks to the modern world with startling directness. In an age of social media, young people are acutely familiar with the experience of performing for an audience -- curating a face for Instagram, projecting confidence online, writing messages that say "loved catching up!" after conversations that felt hollow. The poem's catalogue of social performances -- the smile without feeling, the compliment without sincerity, the welcome without intention -- maps precisely onto the pressures of digital social life, where likes and follows have replaced the warmth of genuine connection. Okara's narrator wears a home face and an office face; today's young person wears a public profile and a private self. The core anxiety is the same: which face is real? The poem's plea -- "show me how to laugh" -- is perhaps even more urgent now. The child in the poem, who still laughs genuinely, is a reminder that authenticity is not lost -- only buried.

questions.q: Describe the ordinary man's memory as Lynd presents it.
questions.ans: Lynd presents the ordinary man's memory as surprisingly efficient. People remember clothing, doors, lights, appointments, addresses, names, and daily duties, though they still forget small things occasionally.

questions.q: Compare poets and statesmen in relation to memory.

questions.q: Why is the baby-in-the-perambulator incident significant?
questions.ans: The incident is the essay's funniest example of extreme absent-mindedness. It shows how rare such forgetfulness is and helps Lynd prove that most people are actually memory-efficient by contrast.

questions.q: How is the theme of forgetfulness treated humorously?
questions.ans: Lynd treats forgetfulness through comic examples like forgotten medicines, unposted letters, lost sports equipment, and the forgotten baby. His tone is gentle, witty, and self-inclusive.

questions.q: What happens to the letter in Lynd's pocket?
questions.ans: After Lynd forgets to post the letter, he puts it into his pocket for safety. It remains there with an "unadventurous life" until discovered later, never reaching its destination.

questions.q: Explain "citizens of dreamland."
questions.ans: "Citizens of dreamland" refers to people whose minds are absorbed in memories, dreams, or imagination. Sportsmen and anglers forget practical objects because they are mentally elsewhere.

questions.q: What is the message of the essay?
questions.ans: The essay teaches us not to exaggerate human forgetfulness. Memory is usually efficient, and some absent-mindedness may come from imagination, dislike, or deep absorption rather than carelessness.

questions.q: How is the essay relevant to students?
questions.ans: Students often forget books, homework, tickets, or deadlines. Lynd's essay helps them laugh at such moments while also understanding the need for attention and methodical habits.

questions.q: Write an essay on Lynd's view of human memory.
questions.ans: Robert Lynd's view of human memory is balanced, humorous, and thoughtful. He begins by saying that the efficiency of memory, not its failure, amazes him. Modern man remembers telephone numbers, addresses, appointments, names, clothing, doors, and lights. Yet Lynd admits that memory fails in small matters such as taking medicines and posting letters. He laughs at himself for forgetting both. He also explains that sportsmen, anglers, and poets may forget ordinary things because their minds are filled with more exciting or glorious thoughts. Thus Lynd does not condemn forgetfulness. He shows that memory is generally reliable, while absent-mindedness is sometimes human, comic, and even imaginative.

questions.q: Explain the theme of forgetfulness in the essay.
questions.ans: The central theme of the essay is forgetfulness, but Lynd treats it in an unusual way. Instead of merely blaming people for forgetting, he first praises the efficiency of memory. People remember countless duties every day. Then he discusses the small areas where memory fails, such as medicines and letters. Psychologists may say we forget things we secretly dislike. Lynd also suggests that some people forget because their minds are absorbed in richer thoughts. Sportsmen, anglers, and poets become 'citizens of dreamland.' The essay shows that forgetfulness may come from dislike, absorption, imagination, or ordinary human weakness.

questions.q: Explain the significance of the unposted letter.
questions.ans: The unposted letter is one of the most memorable comic symbols in the essay. Lynd says that posting letters is the commonest form of forgetfulness. He admits that anyone who asks him to post a letter is a poor judge of character. Even if he carries it in his hand, he passes the pillar-box before remembering. Then he puts the letter into his pocket for safety and forgets it completely. The letter has an "unadventurous life" because it goes nowhere. This example shows how small duties can disappear from the mind, even when we fully intend to do them.

questions.q: Compare ordinary forgetfulness and imaginative absent-mindedness.
questions.ans: Lynd distinguishes ordinary forgetfulness from imaginative absent-mindedness. Ordinary forgetfulness includes failing to take medicine or post letters. These are small practical failures and often cause inconvenience. Imaginative absent-mindedness, however, may come from the mind being absorbed in something richer. Sportsmen forget bats or balls because they are dreaming about the game. Anglers forget fishing-rods while inventing glorious fishing stories. Poets may forget ordinary duties because their minds are filled with artistic material. Lynd calls such absent-mindedness almost a virtue. Through this comparison, he shows that not all forgetfulness is the same.

questions.q: Do you agree that absent-mindedness can be almost a virtue?
questions.ans: I agree with Lynd that some kinds of absent-mindedness can be almost a virtue. If a person forgets duties because of laziness, it is not admirable. But Lynd speaks of people whose minds are filled with something more intense or imaginative. A sportsman may forget a bat because his mind is full of the game. An angler may forget his rod because he is dreaming of his day's sport. A poet may forget to post a letter because his mind is occupied with creative thought. Such forgetfulness shows absorption, imagination, and depth, though it should not become careless irresponsibility.

questions.q: How does Lynd use humour in "Forgetting"?
questions.ans: Lynd uses humour through exaggeration, self-mockery, and surprising examples. He jokes that chemists make fortunes out of medicines people forget to take. He laughs at himself as someone unfit to be trusted with posting letters. The unposted letter leading an "unadventurous life" is a witty personification. The funniest example is the father who forgets his baby outside a public-house and returns home cheerfully asking for lunch. Lynd's humour is gentle, not cruel. It helps readers recognize their own weaknesses without feeling ashamed, and it turns an ordinary topic into a delightful essay.

questions.q: How is "Forgetting" relevant to modern life?
questions.ans: "Forgetting" is highly relevant to modern life because people today handle even more information than before. Students remember passwords, schedules, lessons, phone numbers, messages, and deadlines, but they may still forget a notebook, ticket, birthday, or medicine. Lynd's essay teaches us to see memory fairly. We should not call ourselves failures because of small forgetful moments. At the same time, important duties need method and attention. The essay also reminds us that people absorbed in creativity or work may forget ordinary details. It encourages humour, patience, and better habits in daily life.
